Windows 3.1 was very much alive in the mid-90s. The release of Windows 95 in August of 1995 was only 20 years ago. I was 23 when that happened and was already deep into my programming career. 16-bit software took several years more to finally get left behind. People who worked on these platforms are not really few and far between. We just don't have any real need to use our old skills since hardware, software and OSes have changed. Some of us chose to stay near the action instead of going into management where we'd lose our skills. I'm glad I stayed in the trenches because I can teach young coders that there is more to programming than slapping some frameworks together with a trendy flat UI. Today's software probably won't have a chance to become legacy like this system did because it doesn't last more than a few years at best. It will have to be replaced regularly (with more costs) as the underlying technologies get abandoned and programmers lose interest. One day someone will be faced with trying to keep a Node.js/Angular/jQuery web app alive on an old build of CentOS to keep some mission critical operation alive. It won't be any different a story except for the names of the technologies.
